text: Now Naomi had a relative on her husband's side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go out to the fields and gather the leftover grain behind anyone who will show me kindness." Naomi said to her, "Go ahead, my daughter."
So she went out and began to gather in the fields behind the harvesters. As it happened, she came to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, "The LORD be with you." "The LORD bless you," they answered.
Boaz asked his servant in charge of the harvesters, "Whose young woman is this?"

versions.text: Boaz asked the servant in charge of the harvesters, "Whose young woman is this?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew לְנַעֲרוֹ has the possessive suffix ("his servant"), which also clarifies that the overseer belongs to Boaz's own workforce. The definite article alone loses this.

text: The servant in charge of the harvesters answered, "She is the Moabite woman who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She said, 'Please let me gather and glean among the sheaves behind the harvesters.' She came and has been on her feet from early this morning until now, resting only a little in the shelter."
So Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen to me, my daughter. Don't go to glean in any other field, and don't go away from here. Stay close to my young women.

Keep your eyes on the field where they are harvesting, and follow along behind my young women. I have ordered the men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink the water the men have drawn.

versions.text: Keep your eyes on the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along behind the women. I have ordered the men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink the water the men have drawn."
versions.explanation: As read aloud, "the men are harvesting... behind the women" is confusing, since the Hebrew simply says "the field they are reaping" and then uses a feminine plural ("after them") pointing back to the young women of verse 8. Naming them explicitly removes the apparent contradiction.

text: At this she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?"

Boaz answered her, "I have been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth and came to a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay you for what you have done, and may you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge."
"May I continue to find favor in your eyes, my lord," she said, "for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant—though I am not even equal to one of your servant girls."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here. Have some bread and dip your piece in the wine vinegar." So she sat down beside the harvesters, and he offered her roasted grain. She ate all she wanted and had some left over.
As she got up to glean, Boaz gave orders to his men: "Let her gather even among the sheaves, and don't shame her.
Even pull out some stalks from the bundles for her and leave them for her to gather, and don't rebuke her."

So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she threshed what she had gathered, and it came to about an ephah of barley.[^1]

[^1]: An ephah was roughly twenty-two liters, or about thirty pounds of grain—an unusually large amount for a day's gleaning.

versions.text: So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she threshed what she had gathered, and it came to about an ephah of barley.
versions.explanation: "Ephah" is an unfamiliar measure for hearers; a brief footnote conveys the surprising generosity of the yield without cluttering the read-aloud text.

text: She carried it back to town, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gathered. Ruth also brought out and gave her what she had left over from her meal.

Her mother-in-law asked her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you!" Then Ruth told her mother-in-law about the one she had worked with. "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz," she said.

"Blessed be he by the LORD," Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "who has not stopped showing his kindness to the living and the dead." And she added, "That man is a close relative of ours; he is one of our family redeemers."[^1]

[^1]: A family redeemer was a near relative responsible for buying back a poor relative's land, and for protecting and providing for the family in need.

versions.text: "Blessed be he by the LORD," Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "who has not stopped showing his kindness to the living and the dead." And she added, "That man is a close relative of ours; he is one of our redeemers."
versions.explanation: "Redeemer" standing alone can be heard as a purely theological title; "family redeemer" with a short note preserves the legal-social sense of גֹּאֵל that drives the rest of the book.

text: Then Ruth the Moabite said, "He even told me, 'Stay close to my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'"

versions.text: Then Ruth the Moabite said, "He even told me, 'Stay close to my workers until they have finished my whole harvest.'"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew הַנְּעָרִים is masculine plural ("my young men"). This matters because Naomi immediately responds in verse 22 by urging Ruth to go out with his young women (נַעֲרוֹתָיו); the gender-neutral "workers" erases the deliberate contrast in the dialogue.

text: Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, so that no one may harm you in another field."
So she stayed close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the barley harvest and the wheat harvest were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
